papers.title: Machine-learned spectral PDE solvers for fluids and plasmas
papers.abstract: Sparse regression methods for discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from data are sensitive to observation noise and are not constrained to reproduce the data under forward integration. We address both limitations by performing weak-form discovery in the spatial discretization in which the PDE is solved, learned by differentiating through multistep rollouts anchored at the observed states. The new method, Weak-form Anchored Rollout for PDEs (WARP), produces a machine-learned PDE solver. In this work, we focus on systems amenable to a spectral Galerkin solver. Across eight benchmark fluid and plasma systems, including high-dimensional turbulent simulations, WARP produces numerically stable rollouts from new random initial conditions and substantially improves coefficient recovery, rollout accuracy, and statistical measures compared with a single-step weak-form SINDy baseline.

papers.title: Tractable Inference with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
papers.abstract: Machine-learning surrogates in computational science often require not only accurate predictions but also expectations, variances, conserved integrals, and normalization constants. Conventional neural networks, including Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs), generally evaluate these quantities through Monte Carlo sampling or multidimensional quadrature, making repeated inference costly, particularly in high dimensions. We introduce KANs with Tractable Operators for Uncertainty and Constraints (TOUCKANs), whose finite-degree polynomial outer functions yield a decomposable sum--product representation. Under factorizing input measures, expectations and higher moments then reduce algebraically to deterministic recursions over one-dimensional leaf integrals. Independent and shared inner-block variants form a parameter-efficiency hierarchy, and a universal-approximation proof for its most restricted member extends to the complete class. The same deterministic operators allow conserved integrals and normalization to be imposed throughout training. Across uniform and Gaussian benchmarks through 50 dimensions, deterministic mean and variance errors remained below the median fixed-budget Monte Carlo errors in every case. TOUCKANs also conserved Cahn--Hilliard mass to machine precision and imposed normalization and orthogonality through deterministic moments, enabling joint computation of the lowest four Schr\"odinger eigenpairs in two, three, and five dimensions. TOUCKANs therefore connect KAN approximation with tractable probabilistic circuits, making statistical operators and integral constraints directly available within an expressive neural surrogate.

papers.title: SoLiD26: A First Principles Solid-Liquid Interface Dataset for Machine-learned Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) enable simulations of larger atomistic systems over longer timescales than traditional ab initio methods but require large, diverse training data. Existing datasets lack comprehensive sampling of solid-liquid interfaces, which exhibit complex phenomena such as solvent layering and surface reconstruction critical for energy and catalytic materials. Here, we present SoLiD26, a curated solid-liquid interface dataset of 15.4 million first-principles structures with up to 576 atoms and 15 chemical elements for training and evaluating MLIPs. The structures were compiled from density functional theory (DFT) calculations, with most configurations originating from ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. SoLiD26 includes aqueous coinage metal interfaces, electrode-electrolyte systems, and selected bulk reference structures, calculated with VASP using the PBE functional and D3 dispersion corrections. The application of SoLiD26 for training and evaluating MLIPs is demonstrated with a suite of MACE models on a simple training, validation and test split. This dataset provides a valuable resource for advancing MLIP development targeted at modelling solid-liquid interfaces in electrochemical and catalytic systems.

papers.title: Model-based computational study of reactive fluid systems using transfer operator methods
papers.abstract: In many industrial applications one aims for the design of efficient chemical reactions. This is often done using experimental analysis of the reactors in combination with numerical twins. However, the simultaneous modeling of flow, mixing and chemical reaction remains a complicated task because the computational costs are still significant and oftentimes prohibitive. Here, we model and analyze mixing processes of chemical substances by a transfer operator method using the Lagrangian trajectories of passive particles. In practice, we represent the spatial distributions of the chemical species concentrations by density vectors. These are evolved by means of a stochastic transition matrix, which is obtained as a numerical approximation of a transfer operator. In a further step, we model the reaction of the fluids by specific update rules of the density vectors. The method is applicable for closed and open example systems and different chemical processes such as competitive consecutive reactions. We demonstrate that the dynamic processes are reflected well by this method. Furthermore, we evaluate the interdependence of the reaction fronts with Lagrangian coherent structures which we define using set-oriented methods that also work well on three dimensional data.

papers.title: Exact quantum circuits for a lattice Boltzmann realization of the Dirac equation
papers.abstract: The quantum lattice Boltzmann scheme of Succi and Dellar advances a four-component Dirac spinor on a lattice by a fixed sequence of local, exactly norm-preserving operations: a basis rotation, a collision, a streaming shift, and the inverse rotation. While this correspondence has been noted qualitatively, it has remained unclear whether it can be realized exactly and unitarily as a gate-model quantum circuit. This unitarity is a structural property of the scheme, which should, in principle, enable an operator-by-operator port onto quantum hardware. We give a gate-level construction of every operation of the three-dimensional Dirac QLB scheme: the fixed rotation gates, the collision gate, the streaming shift as a controlled increment on a position register, the position-dependent potential as a phase oracle, and periodic and reflecting boundary conditions as unitary circuits. Together, these constructions provide the first complete demonstration that the scheme is exactly representable in the gate model without any approximation beyond the classical method itself. We then compose them into single-axis, two- and three-dimensional time steps. On a state-vector emulator the resulting circuits reproduce the classical QLB solver to machine precision, thus verifying our quantum implementation. Our aim is representability and correctness rather than computational speedup; questions of state preparation, asymptotic cost, and hardware noise are identified as open avenues for future work. Appendices restore physical units, derive the scheme's Zitterbewegung in closed form and compare it with a trapped-ion simulation, and execute a reduced two-site instance on a Rigetti superconducting processor, where choosing the qubits from the live calibration lowers the state-preparation error. All operators, circuits, and figures are reproducible from the open-source quantumKineticMethods library.

papers.title: Matrix-free phase-field modeling of fracture in micromechanical testing simulations of inelastic materials
papers.abstract: Resolving steep damage gradients across diffuse cracks in the phase-field modeling of fracture favors the use of high-order finite elements, for which matrix-free methods can provide superior performance and scalability. Here, we implement the Peric & Dettmer constitutive framework for visco-elastoplastic materials in an open source solid mechanics library supporting matrix-free operators for high-order finite elements with p-multigrid preconditioning on GPUs. We introduce a rheological fracture element assembled in series with the Peric & Dettmer block, keeping fracture and inelastic material properties mutually independent. We conduct numerical simulations of tensile and compressive quasistatic tests on synthetic particle-matrix microstructures using an El Capitan high-performance computing prototype. The results reproduce representative inelastic responses and fracture patterns, including X-shaped cracking observed in polymer-bonded explosives and cup-and-cone fracture in ductile metals.

papers.title: DiffVortex: A quantum-inspired fast solver for incompressible flows
papers.abstract: Matrix-product-state (MPS) and quantized tensor-train (QTT) representations offer a promising framework for computational fluid dynamics, with logarithmic run time and memory scaling in mesh size when bond dimensions remain bounded. Existing MPS-based solvers are Eulerian: they compress velocity fields and enforce immersed-body boundary conditions through static masks or body-fitted coordinates. Moving or flexible bodies complicate this approach: deformation requires updating MPS masks every time step, while filamentary vorticity in high-Reynolds-number flows may resist low-rank compression. We propose a complementary approach: compress the Biot--Savart kernel rather than the flow state, evolve vorticity using Lagrangian vortex particles, and represent immersed bodies by bound vortex sheets on Lagrangian surface points. Our main theoretical result is a lifting theorem: QTT rank $r$ of the kernel implies matrix-product-operator (MPO) rank at most $2^d r$ for the corresponding convolution operator in $d$ dimensions, independent of grid resolution. This bound is sharp for our interleaved ordering. With quantics tensor cross interpolation, the moment-to-local stage of a single-level fast multipole method becomes a precomputed tensor-network contraction with quasi-linear complexity, retaining Lagrangian flexibility for immersed bodies. Our PyTorch implementation (\texttt{DiffVortex}) is end-to-end differentiable, runs on GPUs, and handles $6.7\times10^{7}$ particles on a single device. We validate against reference vortex-method results for an impulsively started cylinder and exact and reference solutions for inviscid elliptical vortices. We also demonstrate two-dimensional flows past rigidly moving, multiple, and deforming bodies, including gradients propagated through the full time integration.

papers.title: Pushing beyond the memory barrier in propagation algorithms with randomization
papers.abstract: Performant classical tools for simulating quantum circuits are important for benchmarking and supporting upcoming quantum devices. Pauli propagation offers promising capabilities, but deep circuits usually cause a rapid growth in the number of Pauli strings and can quickly exhaust the available memory. In this work, we introduce a randomized protocol that combines a specialized resampling schedule, merging, and a controlled amount of bias to keep the propagating Pauli sum within any prescribed memory budget. Additional computational resources can then be spent on embarrassingly parallel repetitions that systematically improve the estimate. Building on the open-source library PauliPropagation.jl, we show that 1) increasing memory of each simulation reduces the error systematically more than outside averaging, 2) resampling just enough to apply the next gate delays variance accumulation and gives better error-per-time trade-offs than more aggressive resampling, and 3) a small, controlled bias is crucial in cutting down variance and pushing far beyond unbiased randomization. The resulting framework can reproduce deterministic calculations while requiring several orders of magnitude less memory.

papers.title: A Reproducible Benchmark and Evidence-Retrieval Software Framework for Silicon Detector R&D Literature
papers.abstract: Silicon pixel detector R&D depends on a large and rapidly growing technical literature, including beam-test and irradiation studies, performance measurements, simulation, and design reports. Locating the supporting evidence passage for a measurement, operating condition, or design decision is therefore a computing and data-science challenge for detector-development workflows. General-purpose language models are insufficient unless grounded in traceable primary sources, particularly in a domain with specialised terminology, configuration-dependent measurements, and rapidly evolving experimental results. We address this with a reproducible, general-purpose framework for evidence-grounded retrieval over technical literature, using silicon pixel detector R&D as a demanding validation domain. The framework combines sparse lexical retrieval, dense semantic retrieval, and hybrid reciprocal-rank fusion, with an optional graph-guided exploration layer and grounded, abstention-aware response generation. The accompanying benchmark provides manually curated chunk-level evidence annotations, source-level diagnostics, semantic relevance checks, and negative-query abstention tests over two detector query sets. We evaluate six retrieval configurations across 378 source documents and 8,442 indexed chunks. Hybrid sparse-dense retrieval gives the strongest strict evidence recovery, achieving Hit@5 of 0.917 on the core benchmark and 0.951 on the curated extension benchmark, while graph-based methods are more effective for literature exploration and source discovery. Graph expansion is therefore best employed as a discovery layer over the hybrid retrieval backbone. The framework provides reusable software for traceable, 1 evidence-grounded knowledge access in silicon detector R&D and high-energy physics instrumentation.

papers.title: Fast Evaluation of the Sixth-Order Time-Convolutionless (TCL6) Master-Equation Generator
papers.abstract: Higher-order time-convolutionless (TCL) master equations provide systematic corrections for non-Markovian dynamics in open quantum systems, but their time-ordered integrals become increasingly costly to evaluate. Direct quadrature of the Hadamard-reduced sixth-order (TCL6) generator at all $N_t$ sampled times requires $O(N_t^3)$ operations at fixed system dimension. We derive an exact reduction for a finite-dimensional system coupled through one Hermitian operator to a stationary centered Gaussian bath. By separating operator coefficients from scalar time-dependent spectral densities, the complete TCL6 time series is reduced to cumulative sums and first-order recurrences, one-dimensional causal convolutions, and an exact dyadic recursion for interlocked sums. With the algorithm, evaluating the complete TCL6 time series requires $O(N_t\log^2N_t)$ operations. These reductions enable fast, practical simulations of non-Markovian dynamics involving multiphonon and multiphoton processes in open quantum systems.

papers.title: Euclidean Fourier Neural Operators
papers.abstract: Fourier neural operators (FNOs) provide an efficient framework for learning mappings between function spaces as they are, by construction, independent of the grid resolution at which they are trained and evaluated. However, FNOs are not independent of the periodic domain they are applied to: their discrete spectral weights are indexed by integer Fourier mode numbers, which correspond to physical wavevectors. When applied to a different domain, the same trained weights act at different wavevectors, and the FNO silently represents a different operator. This makes FNOs unsuitable for tasks where transfer across domains is crucial. We propose Euclidean Fourier neural operators~(EFNOs) as a domain-independent alternative to FNOs. By parameterizing the spectral kernel as a continuous function of the physical wavevector, the EFNO can learn operators that act consistently across periodic domains of varying shape and size. We evaluate the EFNO on a simple heat equation and on a practically relevant materials science task of learning exchange-correlation potentials across different crystal structures, and demonstrate that the EFNO is able to generalize to unseen grid sizes and domains.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal spin transport from first principles
papers.abstract: Manipulating spin for quantum information and spintronic devices requires quantitative prediction of quantum transport over long time and length scales. We introduce a computational framework for first-principles density-matrix quantum transport within the Wigner function formalism that facilitates spin dynamics and transport simulations, while accounting for electron-phonon scattering at device length scales. This allows us to elucidate the impact of realistic spin-orbit fields, such as Rashba and persistent spin helix, on coherent spin transport in several materials, as well as the transition to incoherent transport with increasing strength of electron-phonon scattering. We identify three distinct regimes of incoherent spin transport corresponding to the free induction decay, Dyakonov-Perel and Elliott-Yafet regimes of spin relaxation, and find a scattering-strength-independent spin diffusion length within the Dyakonov-Perel regime. With applied magnetic fields, spin transport in this regime is sensitive to scattering strength and leads to asymmetric Hanle curves that probe the internal spin-orbit field of the material.

papers.title: Hybrid ensemble forecasting combining physics-based and machine-learning predictions through spectral nudging
papers.abstract: We present the first application of spectral nudging in a probabilistic ensemble forecasting framework, combining the physics-based ECMWF Integrated Forecasting System ensemble (IFS-ENS) with forecasts from the probabilistic machine-learned AIFS-ENS ensemble. Large scales of virtual temperature and vorticity are relaxed toward the machine-learned forecasts, while mesoscale structures remain governed by the physics-based model. This hybrid ensemble shows substantial improvements in large-scale forecast skill, with gains in predictive skill extended by up to two days in the tropics and by approximately half a day in the extra-tropics relative to IFS-ENS. Despite nudging being applied only to upper-air fields, improvements are also found in several near-surface parameters. Tropical cyclone track forecasts improve significantly, consistent with improved representation of the large-scale steering flow, without degrading storm intensity or ensemble spread. These results demonstrate that spectral nudging can be successfully extended to ensemble prediction and provide an attractive pathway for combining machine-learned and physics-based weather prediction systems.
